{{short description|American journalist and recreational mathematician}}
'''Gary Antonick''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|æ|n|t|ə|n|ɪ|k}} {{Respell|AN|tə|nik}};<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fLCWx7Dr2gg|title=The Neuroscience of Curiosity by Gary Antonick|website=[[YouTube]] |date=22 October 2014 |accessdate=22 May 2020}}</ref> born February 11, 1963) is an American journalist and recreational mathematician who for many years wrote a puzzle-based column called "Numberplay" for the [[New York Times]].<ref name=square/>

==Education and career==
Antonick has a BS in Engineering from the [[University of Michigan]] and an MBA from [[Harvard Business School]].<ref name=stanford>[https://web.stanford.edu/~antonick/ Gary Antonick] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129102017/http://web.stanford.edu/~antonick/ |date=2019-01-29 }} Stanford University Human Sciences and Technologies Advanced Research Institute</ref> In 2019, he taught a course at [[Stanford University]], titled ''Math in the Wild: Using Mathematical Thinking to Solve Messy Real-World Problems'', alongside [[Keith Devlin]].<ref>[https://www.eduexplora.com/beyondtherules/ Gary Antonick: MBA, Stanford University & Harvard University]</ref>

==Numberplay==
From December 2009 to October 2016 Antonick wrote the puzzle themed "Numberplay" column for ''The New York Times''.<ref name=farewell>''[https://www.nytimes.com/2016/10/31/crosswords/gary-antonick-numberplay-farewell.html?rref=collection%2Fcolumn%2Fnumberplay&action=click&contentCollection=crosswords&region=stream&module=stream_unit&version=latest&contentPlacement=1&pgtype=collection A Numberplay Farewell]'' Gary Antonick, New York Times, October 31, 2016. Outgoing writer of The Times’s Numberplay column, shares a lesson learned from seven years of puzzle-solving.</ref> The puzzles generally involved math or logic problems.<ref name=square>[https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/04/08/squareable/?mtrref=www.google.com%20Numberplay:%20The%20Squareable%20Puzzle About numberplay, the puzzle suite for math lovers of all ages] by Gary Antonick, The New York Times, April 8, 2013</ref> They came from many sources, and many were descended from columns by the celebrated [[Scientific American]] columnist [[Martin Gardner]].<ref name=gardner>''[http://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/11/30/gardner-impromptu/ Martin Gardner’s Impromptu]'' By Gary Antonick, New York Times, November 30, 2015</ref> He often wrote about Gardner and considered him to be the leading popularizer of [[recreational mathematics]].<ref name=coconuts>''[https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/10/07/gardner-2/ Martin Gardner’s The Monkey and the Coconuts]'' "Martin Gardner, the American science and math writer who popularized the notion of recreational mathematics." in Numberplay The ''New York Times'':, October 7, 2013</ref><ref>''[https://www.maa.org/news/math-news/martin-gardner-hated-doing-puzzles-says-diaconis Martin Gardner Hated Doing Puzzles, Says Diaconis]'' [[Mathematical Association of America]], October 15, 2014</ref> Conferences called [[Gathering 4 Gardner]] are held every two years to celebrate Gardner's legacy, and Antonick has twice spoken at these events.<ref name=curiosity>''[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fLCWx7Dr2gg The Neuroscience of Curiosity]'' video by Gary Antonick, G4G Celebration published on Oct 22, 2014</ref><ref name=projectile>''[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4uc5xzFXm4c Projectile on an Incline-No Calculation]'' video by Gary Antonick, G4G Celebration, Published on Jul 19, 2018</ref> He also supports the [[Julia Robinson Mathematics Festival]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.jrmf.org/support-jrmf/sponsors-and-partners/ |title=Friends of JRMF |access-date=2019-04-23 |archive-date=2019-04-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190415173301/https://www.jrmf.org/support-jrmf/sponsors-and-partners/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Among the many classic problems of recreational mathematics featured in "Numberplay" are The [[Prisoner's Dilemma]], The [[Two child problem|Two Child Problem]], The [[Monty Hall Problem]], The [[Monkey and the coconuts|Monkey and the Coconuts]], [[The Two-cube calendar|The Two-cube Calendar]], and [[The Zebra Puzzle]]. Sometimes "Numberplay" was used to celebrate other mathematicians such as Paul Erdős,<ref name=erdos>''[https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/03/25/erdos/ The Improbable Life of Paul Erdős]'' in Numberplay The ''New York Times'', March 25, 2013</ref> or simply to report a breakthrough in mathematics or game theory.<ref name=go>''[https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2016/02/01/brilliant-go/ Google Artificial Intelligence Beats Expert at Go Game]'' by Gary Antonick, February 1, 2016</ref>

"Numberplay" columns led to five sequences originated by Antonick<ref>OEIS sequence numbers A227050, A051732, A247653, A247654, and A240567</ref> being listed in the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] (OEIS)<ref name=OEIS>[https://oeis.org/search?q=Antonick&sort=&language=english&go=Search Sequences originated by Gary Antonick] [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]]</ref>

==English Channel Swim==
On August 8, 1988, Antonick swam the English Channel, starting from Dover, England, and finishing in France 8 hours and 46 minutes later. <ref>{{cite web |title=Photograph of Gary Antonick U. S. A. |url=https://www.channelswimmingdover.org.uk/content/photo/photograph-of-gary-antonick-u-s-a |access-date=2023-06-15 |website=Channel Swimming Dover}}</ref>
